questions.text: What is the main job of an operating-system kernel?
options: Manage hardware resources and offer core services to programs
Store all websites on the internet
questions.correctAnswer: Manage hardware resources and offer core services to programs
questions.explanation:
The kernel is the core of an operating system that manages processes, memory and hardware access.

Why: Applications use system calls to request operating-system services.

Example: The kernel controls access to CPU time and physical memory.

Student note: A shell is an interface to the OS; it is not the same thing as the kernel.

study.title: Kernel
study.simple: The kernel is the core of an operating system that manages processes, memory and hardware access.
steps: Applications use system calls to request operating-system services.
study.example: The kernel controls access to CPU time and physical memory.
study.pitfall: A shell is an interface to the OS; it is not the same thing as the kernel.
study.remember: Applications use system calls to request operating-system services.

keyTerms.meaning: The kernel is the core of an operating system that manages processes, memory and hardware access.

whyCorrect: The kernel is the privileged core that sits between applications and the hardware. It decides how CPU time, memory, devices and other resources are shared, and programs request those services through system calls. That is exactly why managing hardware resources and providing core services is the best answer.
notes: Applications normally run in user space and cannot directly control protected hardware whenever they want.
Process scheduling, virtual memory, device drivers and access control are major kernel responsibilities.
A shell such as Bash is a user program that accepts commands; it uses kernel services rather than replacing the kernel.

questions.text: Which statement best describes a Linux distribution?
options: A kernel plus a selected set of tools, packages and configuration
questions.correctAnswer: A kernel plus a selected set of tools, packages and configuration
questions.explanation:
A distribution combines the Linux kernel with user-space software and package management.

Why: Different distributions make different packaging and support choices.

Example: Ubuntu and Fedora both distribute Linux with differing package tools.

Student note: Do not assume commands for one distro apply to every other distro.

study.title: Linux distribution
study.simple: A distribution combines the Linux kernel with user-space software and package management.
steps: Different distributions make different packaging and support choices.
study.example: Ubuntu and Fedora both distribute Linux with differing package tools.
study.pitfall: Do not assume commands for one distro apply to every other distro.
study.remember: Different distributions make different packaging and support choices.

keyTerms.meaning: A distribution combines the Linux kernel with user-space software and package management.

whyCorrect: Linux by itself refers to the kernel. A usable distribution packages that kernel together with user-space commands, libraries, installers, a package manager, defaults and configuration. Therefore the answer correctly describes the complete system people install as Ubuntu, Fedora and similar distributions.
notes: Different distributions can use the same Linux kernel family but provide different package formats and administration tools.
Debian/Ubuntu commonly use APT and .deb packages; Fedora/RHEL-family systems commonly use DNF/RPM.
When an exam asks about a distribution, think: kernel + software + package management + configuration.

questions.text: Which kind of freedom is normally associated with open-source software?
options: Permission to inspect and modify source under licence terms
The right to ignore all licences
questions.correctAnswer: Permission to inspect and modify source under licence terms
questions.explanation:
Open-source licences give specified rights to inspect, use, change and redistribute software.

Why: The licence terms still apply when software is copied or shared.

Example: Developers can inspect source code for a released component.

Student note: 'Free' in free software is about freedom, not necessarily zero price.

study.title: Open source
study.simple: Open-source licences give specified rights to inspect, use, change and redistribute software.
steps: The licence terms still apply when software is copied or shared.
study.example: Developers can inspect source code for a released component.
study.pitfall: 'Free' in free software is about freedom, not necessarily zero price.
study.remember: The licence terms still apply when software is copied or shared.

keyTerms.meaning: Open-source licences give specified rights to inspect, use, change and redistribute software.

whyCorrect: Open-source software makes its source code available under a licence that grants defined rights such as inspection, modification and redistribution. Those rights come from the licence, so the freedom is not permission to ignore copyright or licence conditions.
notes: Open source does not automatically mean 'no cost'; software may still be sold.
The exact rights and obligations depend on the specific licence.
Copyright still exists; the licence tells users what they are allowed to do with the copyrighted work.

questions.text: Which pair correctly contrasts MIT-style permissive licensing with GPL-style copyleft?
options: MIT generally gives broad reuse with notices; GPL has stronger conditions for certain distributed derivative works
MIT bans all modifications; GPL bans source access
Both automatically put work in the public domain
questions.correctAnswer: MIT generally gives broad reuse with notices; GPL has stronger conditions for certain distributed derivative works
questions.explanation:
Open-source licences vary in how they require notices and downstream licensing.

Why: Permissive terms are generally lighter than strong copyleft distribution conditions.

Example: An organisation inventories licences before shipping a product.

Student note: Always read the exact licence and version rather than relying on a slogan.

study.title: Licence models
study.simple: Open-source licences vary in how they require notices and downstream licensing.
steps: Permissive terms are generally lighter than strong copyleft distribution conditions.
study.example: An organisation inventories licences before shipping a product.
study.pitfall: Always read the exact licence and version rather than relying on a slogan.
study.remember: Permissive terms are generally lighter than strong copyleft distribution conditions.

keyTerms.meaning: Open-source licences vary in how they require notices and downstream licensing.

whyCorrect: MIT-style licences are permissive: they generally allow broad reuse, including in proprietary products, as long as required notices are kept. GPL-style licences are copyleft: when covered derivative work is distributed, stronger source-code and same-licence obligations can apply. That is the key contrast in the correct option.
notes: Permissive licence = few downstream restrictions compared with strong copyleft.
Copyleft does not ban commercial use; GPL software can be sold.
Always distinguish using software privately from distributing a modified or combined work, because distribution often triggers licence obligations.

questions.text: On a Debian/Ubuntu-style system, what is apt update generally used for?
questions.explanation:
Package managers use repository metadata to learn which versions are available.

Why: apt update refreshes metadata; it does not by itself upgrade every installed package.

Example: An administrator can refresh indexes before installing a package.

Student note: Other Linux distributions may use dnf or another package manager.

study.title: Package indexes
study.simple: Package managers use repository metadata to learn which versions are available.
steps: apt update refreshes metadata; it does not by itself upgrade every installed package.
study.example: An administrator can refresh indexes before installing a package.
study.pitfall: Other Linux distributions may use dnf or another package manager.
study.remember: apt update refreshes metadata; it does not by itself upgrade every installed package.

keyTerms.meaning: Package managers use repository metadata to learn which versions are available.

whyCorrect: APT uses package indexes to know what packages and versions repositories currently offer. apt update downloads fresh repository metadata; it does not itself install all available upgrades. That is why 'refresh available package indexes' is correct.
notes: Typical sequence: apt update first, then apt upgrade or apt install as needed.
The package index is metadata about packages, not the installed package files themselves.
If the index is stale, the system may not know about newly published versions.

questions.text: Which command prints the working directory?
questions.explanation:
The working directory is the location a shell treats as the base for relative paths.

Why: pwd prints that location.

Example: A terminal may print /home/student/projects.

Student note: cd changes directories; pwd reports the current directory.

study.title: pwd
study.simple: The working directory is the location a shell treats as the base for relative paths.
steps: pwd prints that location.
study.pitfall: cd changes directories; pwd reports the current directory.

keyTerms.meaning: The working directory is the location a shell treats as the base for relative paths.

whyCorrect: pwd means 'print working directory'. The shell always has a current working directory, and pwd displays its absolute path, so it directly answers the question.
notes: The working directory is the starting point used to resolve relative paths.
cd changes the working directory; pwd reports it.
A command such as pwd may return a path like /home/student/projects.

questions.text: When you are in /home/student, which is an absolute filesystem path?
questions.explanation:
An absolute path begins at the root directory /; a relative path begins from the current location.

Why: /var/log/syslog identifies a path independently of your current directory.

Example: The same relative filename can refer to different files after cd.

Student note: ~ expands to a home directory in many shells, but / marks the filesystem root.

study.title: Absolute paths
study.simple: An absolute path begins at the root directory /; a relative path begins from the current location.
steps: /var/log/syslog identifies a path independently of your current directory.
study.example: The same relative filename can refer to different files after cd.
study.pitfall: ~ expands to a home directory in many shells, but / marks the filesystem root.
study.remember: /var/log/syslog identifies a path independently of your current directory.

keyTerms.meaning: An absolute path begins at the root directory /; a relative path begins from the current location.

whyCorrect: An absolute path starts from the filesystem root, written as /. /var/log/syslog starts with /, so it identifies the same location regardless of the current directory. The other options are relative forms whose meaning depends on where you are.
notes: ../ means the parent of the current directory.
./ means the current directory.
A path that begins with / is the quickest exam clue that it is absolute.

questions.text: Which command creates nested directories such as work/2026/notes even when the parents do not exist?
questions.explanation:
mkdir creates directories; -p creates missing parent directories as needed.

Why: It avoids failures when intermediate directories are absent.

Example: mkdir -p lab/linux/partitions prepares a nested folder.

Student note: Creating a folder is not the same as mounting a filesystem there.

study.title: mkdir -p
study.simple: mkdir creates directories; -p creates missing parent directories as needed.
steps: It avoids failures when intermediate directories are absent.
study.example: mkdir -p lab/linux/partitions prepares a nested folder.
study.pitfall: Creating a folder is not the same as mounting a filesystem there.
study.remember: It avoids failures when intermediate directories are absent.

keyTerms.meaning: mkdir creates directories; -p creates missing parent directories as needed.

whyCorrect: mkdir creates directories and the -p option tells it to create missing parent directories too. Therefore mkdir -p work/2026/notes can create the whole path even when work and work/2026 do not yet exist.
notes: Without -p, mkdir normally fails if a required parent directory does not exist.
With -p, existing parent directories are not treated as an error.
Creating a directory only creates a folder entry; it does not create or mount a new filesystem.

questions.text: Which command displays hidden entries along with normal entries in the current directory?
questions.explanation:
Unix-like systems normally hide names beginning with a dot in basic ls output.

Why: ls -a includes those entries.

Example: The .bashrc file becomes visible with ls -a ~.

Student note: Hidden is a display convention, not an encryption or security feature.

study.title: Hidden files
study.simple: Unix-like systems normally hide names beginning with a dot in basic ls output.
steps: ls -a includes those entries.
study.example: The .bashrc file becomes visible with ls -a ~.
study.pitfall: Hidden is a display convention, not an encryption or security feature.

keyTerms.meaning: Unix-like systems normally hide names beginning with a dot in basic ls output.

whyCorrect: Linux and other Unix-like systems treat names beginning with . as hidden from the normal ls display. The -a option means 'all', so ls -a includes dotfiles as well as ordinary entries.
notes: Examples of dotfiles include .bashrc and .profile.
Hidden files are not protected merely because they begin with a dot.
ls -la combines hidden entries with the detailed long-listing format.

questions.text: What does the numeric file mode 640 mean for a regular file?
options: Owner read/write, group read, others no access
questions.correctAnswer: Owner read/write, group read, others no access
questions.explanation:
Numeric modes combine read=4, write=2 and execute=1 for owner, group and others.

Why: 6 is rw-, 4 is r--, 0 is ---.

Example: chmod 640 report.txt restricts report access.

Student note: Permissions on a directory have different practical effects, especially execute/traversal.

study.title: chmod 640
study.simple: Numeric modes combine read=4, write=2 and execute=1 for owner, group and others.
steps: 6 is rw-, 4 is r--, 0 is ---.
study.pitfall: Permissions on a directory have different practical effects, especially execute/traversal.

keyTerms.meaning: Numeric modes combine read=4, write=2 and execute=1 for owner, group and others.

whyCorrect: Numeric permissions are read=4, write=2 and execute=1. For 640, owner gets 6 = 4+2 = read/write, group gets 4 = read only, and others get 0 = no permissions. That exactly matches the correct option.
notes: Read the three digits as owner, group, others.
7=rwx, 6=rw-, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=--- are useful patterns to memorise.
For directories, read/write/execute have different practical meanings from regular files, especially execute meaning traversal.

questions.text: Which command changes file ownership from root to account student (with a suitable privilege)?
questions.explanation:
A Linux file records an owning user and an owning group.

Why: chown changes ownership when the caller has permission.

Example: sudo chown student:project report.txt sets user and group.

Student note: chmod changes mode bits; chown changes ownership.

study.title: chown
study.simple: A Linux file records an owning user and an owning group.
steps: chown changes ownership when the caller has permission.
study.example: sudo chown student:project report.txt sets user and group.
study.pitfall: chmod changes mode bits; chown changes ownership.
study.remember: chown changes ownership when the caller has permission.

keyTerms.meaning: A Linux file records an owning user and an owning group.

whyCorrect: chown means 'change owner'. chown student report.txt changes the owning user of report.txt to student when the caller has sufficient privilege. The other commands inspect, print or search data rather than changing ownership.
notes: chown user:group file can change both owner and group in one command.
chmod changes permission bits; chown changes ownership.
Changing ownership normally requires root or suitable administrative privilege.

questions.text: Which statement about an inode is most accurate for a typical Unix filesystem?
options: It stores file metadata and points to file data, but the filename lives in directory entries
It is the same thing as the file extension
It is always the file's password
questions.correctAnswer: It stores file metadata and points to file data, but the filename lives in directory entries
questions.explanation:
An inode records metadata such as ownership, permissions and data locations.

Why: Directories associate names with inode numbers.

Example: Two hard links can refer to one inode.

Student note: Inode exhaustion can prevent new files even when storage space remains.

study.title: Inodes
study.simple: An inode records metadata such as ownership, permissions and data locations.
steps: Directories associate names with inode numbers.
study.example: Two hard links can refer to one inode.
study.pitfall: Inode exhaustion can prevent new files even when storage space remains.
study.remember: Directories associate names with inode numbers.

keyTerms.meaning: An inode records metadata such as ownership, permissions and data locations.

whyCorrect: An inode stores filesystem metadata such as owner, permissions, timestamps and references to the file's data blocks. The filename is stored in a directory entry that maps a name to an inode number, so the correct option describes the separation accurately.
notes: A file can have more than one filename through hard links because multiple directory entries can reference the same inode.
The inode normally does not contain the ordinary filename itself.
A filesystem can run out of inodes even when some disk space remains.

questions.text: What distinguishes a symbolic link from a hard link?
options: A symbolic link stores a target path and can become dangling if the target is removed
Symbolic links always duplicate file bytes
Hard links always cross every filesystem
Symbolic links are a kind of encryption
questions.correctAnswer: A symbolic link stores a target path and can become dangling if the target is removed
questions.explanation:
A symbolic link points to a pathname rather than sharing exactly the same inode like a typical hard link.

Why: Its path may stop resolving when the target is renamed or deleted.

Example: ln -s /srv/data/current shortcut creates a symlink.

Student note: Ordinary hard links to files normally cannot span different filesystems.

study.title: Symbolic links
study.simple: A symbolic link points to a pathname rather than sharing exactly the same inode like a typical hard link.
steps: Its path may stop resolving when the target is renamed or deleted.
study.pitfall: Ordinary hard links to files normally cannot span different filesystems.
study.remember: Its path may stop resolving when the target is renamed or deleted.

keyTerms.meaning: A symbolic link points to a pathname rather than sharing exactly the same inode like a typical hard link.

whyCorrect: A symbolic link stores a pathname to another object. If that target path no longer exists, the symlink remains but becomes dangling. A hard link instead creates another directory entry for the same inode, which is why the correct answer focuses on the stored path and possible dangling link.
notes: Symlinks can usually point across filesystems; ordinary hard links cannot.
Deleting the original filename does not destroy file data if another hard link still references the inode.
ln -s target linkname creates a symbolic link.

questions.text: What does export NAME=value do in Bash?
options: Makes NAME available in the current shell environment and to its subsequently launched child processes
Writes NAME to the partition table
questions.correctAnswer: Makes NAME available in the current shell environment and to its subsequently launched child processes
questions.explanation:
Shell variables are not automatically passed to every child process; exported variables join the environment.

Why: export marks or sets a variable for inheritance by subsequently launched commands.

Example: export EDITOR=nano lets child tools see the EDITOR choice.

Student note: Changes made by a child process generally do not rewrite the parent's environment.

study.title: Exported variables
study.simple: Shell variables are not automatically passed to every child process; exported variables join the environment.
steps: export marks or sets a variable for inheritance by subsequently launched commands.
study.example: export EDITOR=nano lets child tools see the EDITOR choice.
study.pitfall: Changes made by a child process generally do not rewrite the parent's environment.
study.remember: export marks or sets a variable for inheritance by subsequently launched commands.

keyTerms.meaning: Shell variables are not automatically passed to every child process; exported variables join the environment.

whyCorrect: A normal shell variable belongs to the current shell. export marks the variable for inclusion in the environment passed to commands launched afterwards, so child processes can read NAME=value. That inheritance is the key reason the answer is correct.
notes: Parent-to-child environment inheritance happens when a process starts a child.
A child process normally cannot change the already-running parent's environment.
export NAME=value both assigns the value and exports it in Bash.

questions.text: Which command best shows ownership, mode bits and sizes for entries in a directory?
questions.explanation:
The -l form of ls displays file type, mode bits, ownership, size and timestamps.

Why: It is useful when diagnosing file access.

Example: ls -la includes hidden files and their detailed listing.

Student note: A trailing + indicates you should also consider an ACL.

study.title: Long listing
study.simple: The -l form of ls displays file type, mode bits, ownership, size and timestamps.
steps: It is useful when diagnosing file access.
study.example: ls -la includes hidden files and their detailed listing.
study.pitfall: A trailing + indicates you should also consider an ACL.
study.remember: It is useful when diagnosing file access.

keyTerms.meaning: The -l form of ls displays file type, mode bits, ownership, size and timestamps.

whyCorrect: ls -l requests the long listing format, which displays the file type/mode string, link count, owner, group, size and timestamp. Those are exactly the ownership, mode and size details asked for.
notes: The first character indicates file type; the next nine characters show owner/group/other mode bits.
Use ls -la when you also need hidden entries.
A trailing + after mode bits can indicate additional ACL information.

questions.text: A shared project directory should stop ordinary users deleting each other's files even though all can create new files there. Which mechanism is relevant?
questions.explanation:
The sticky bit adds deletion restrictions on shared writable directories.

Why: It can allow users to create entries without freely removing other users' entries.

Example: /tmp is a familiar example.

Student note: A directory's sticky bit is about deletion/renaming control, not encrypting file contents.

study.title: Shared-directory sticky bit
study.simple: The sticky bit adds deletion restrictions on shared writable directories.
steps: It can allow users to create entries without freely removing other users' entries.
study.pitfall: A directory's sticky bit is about deletion/renaming control, not encrypting file contents.
study.remember: It can allow users to create entries without freely removing other users' entries.

keyTerms.meaning: The sticky bit adds deletion restrictions on shared writable directories.

whyCorrect: On a world- or group-writable shared directory, the sticky bit restricts deletion or renaming so ordinary users cannot freely remove other users' files. It keeps shared creation possible while protecting ownership boundaries, which matches the scenario.
notes: The classic example is /tmp, commonly shown with a final t in its permission string.
The sticky bit acts on directory entry deletion/renaming, not on file encryption.
It is different from setgid, which is mainly used to make new entries inherit the directory's group.

questions.text: Scenario: A college receives 12 Linux laptops for a shared lab. Describe an initial setup checklist covering desktop usability, updates, user accounts, storage and software licensing.
questions.correctAnswer: Choose a supported distribution/desktop; verify hardware/graphics/network; update repository indexes and packages following policy; create standard user accounts with least privilege; plan partitions and backups; test normal/accessible GNOME features/extensions; document installed software and comply with its licences; check security and a rollback plan.
questions.aiReferenceNotes: Reliable Linux setup involves more than the initial operating-system installation. Check hardware requirements and the users' desktop needs. Prepare updates, accounts, permissions and storage safely. Verify applications, backups and licence obligations before handover. A pilot laptop should be checked before repeating the process on the other 11 machines. Do not assume that open-source means no licence obligations or that every user needs sudo.
questions.explanation:
Reliable Linux setup involves more than the initial operating-system installation.

Method:
1. Check hardware requirements and the users' desktop needs.
2. Prepare updates, accounts, permissions and storage safely.
3. Verify applications, backups and licence obligations before handover.

Example: A pilot laptop should be checked before repeating the process on the other 11 machines.

Student note: Do not assume that open-source means no licence obligations or that every user needs sudo.

study.title: Lab setup scenario
study.simple: Reliable Linux setup involves more than the initial operating-system installation.
study.stepsTitle: How to work through this scenario
steps: Check hardware requirements and the users' desktop needs.
Prepare updates, accounts, permissions and storage safely.
Verify applications, backups and licence obligations before handover.
study.example: A pilot laptop should be checked before repeating the process on the other 11 machines.
study.pitfall: Do not assume that open-source means no licence obligations or that every user needs sudo.
study.remember: Check hardware requirements and the users' desktop needs.

keyTerms.meaning: Reliable Linux setup involves more than the initial operating-system installation.

whyCorrect: The scenario asks for a safe lab deployment, so the answer covers the major dependencies in the right order: supported OS/desktop and hardware first, then updates, accounts and least privilege, then storage/backups, required software and licence compliance, followed by testing and rollback. A checklist that ignores any of these leaves a real operational risk.
notes: Start with one pilot laptop before repeating the build across all 12 machines.
Least privilege means normal learners should not receive administrator rights unless they genuinely need them.
Document the build so another technician can reproduce, support or roll back the setup.

questions.text: Scenario: Three tutors must edit files in a shared directory, while learners may read them but must not change them. Describe a practical Linux permission plan and how you would test it.
questions.correctAnswer: Create groups such as tutors and learners; choose directory owner/group; use group permissions, setgid and ACLs if needed to grant tutors write and learners read/traversal while preventing unintended write; use suitable default ACLs for newly created files; check the ACL mask and umask interactions; verify as each type of account.
aiRubric: Considers setgid or default ACL inheritance
questions.aiReferenceNotes: Unix permissions and ACLs help control who may read, change or enter a shared folder. Map required permissions by role before changing modes. Apply ownership, group bits and ACL/default ACL rules as needed. Test creating, reading and editing with representative accounts. getfacl can reveal permissions that are not fully visible in ls -l. Remember directory execute means traversal; reading a directory and reading files within it are separate rights.
questions.explanation:
Unix permissions and ACLs help control who may read, change or enter a shared folder.

Method:
1. Map required permissions by role before changing modes.
2. Apply ownership, group bits and ACL/default ACL rules as needed.
3. Test creating, reading and editing with representative accounts.

Example: getfacl can reveal permissions that are not fully visible in ls -l.

Student note: Remember directory execute means traversal; reading a directory and reading files within it are separate rights.

study.title: Shared-folder permissions
study.simple: Unix permissions and ACLs help control who may read, change or enter a shared folder.
study.stepsTitle: How to work through this scenario
steps: Map required permissions by role before changing modes.
Apply ownership, group bits and ACL/default ACL rules as needed.
Test creating, reading and editing with representative accounts.
study.example: getfacl can reveal permissions that are not fully visible in ls -l.
study.pitfall: Remember directory execute means traversal; reading a directory and reading files within it are separate rights.
study.remember: Map required permissions by role before changing modes.

keyTerms.meaning: Unix permissions and ACLs help control who may read, change or enter a shared folder.

whyCorrect: The requirement is role-based: tutors need write access while learners need read/traverse only. Linux groups provide the broad roles, setgid can preserve the shared group on new files, and ACL/default ACL entries can provide precise and inherited permissions. Testing with representative tutor and learner accounts proves the effective permissions rather than trusting the configuration alone.
notes: Directory execute permission means the ability to traverse/access entries; directory read controls listing names.
Default ACLs affect newly created entries inside a directory; normal ACLs affect the directory or file itself.
The ACL mask can reduce the effective permissions granted to named users or groups, so check getfacl output.
